history.title: Rules Week

data.body:
**Due:** (your teacher will tell you)

Every place you go has rules. This week you find out why.

1. Read **Why We Have Rules** with a grown-up or a partner.
2. Learn the words in **Rule Words**, then win the **Matching** game and the **Memory** game.
3. Look at the **A Good Rule** chart.
4. Sort the cards in **Safe or Fair?**
5. Take **Rules Check** — say each answer out loud first.
6. Lock it in with **Remember the Rule Test**.
7. Read **Rule Questions Kids Ask**.
8. Finish with **Investigation: One Better Rule**.

Your job this week: watch for one rule that helps and one rule you want to ask about. 📋

history.title: Why We Have Rules
history.data:
## Why We Have Rules

Think about your day. You line up. You raise a hand. You walk in the hall. Those are **rules**.

A rule is something we all agree to do. It is not just one person telling you what to do. It is a plan we **share**.

Why do we need them? Try to picture a game with no rules. Everyone grabs the ball. Nobody knows whose **turn** it is. The game stops being fun very fast.

Most rules do one of two jobs.

Some rules keep us **safe**. We hold the rail on the stairs. We stop at the curb. Those rules are about bodies.

Some rules keep things **fair**. We take turns on the swing. We **share** the markers. Those rules are about people getting the same chance.

Here is a good question to ask about any rule. Who does this rule help?

Sometimes a rule helps everyone. Sometimes a rule only helps one person. That second kind is worth asking about.

Rules can change. Grown-ups change them. Kids can ask for a change too. In a lot of places, people **vote** to decide.

Asking about a rule is not the same as breaking it. You can follow a rule today and still ask for a better one tomorrow.

questions.question: What is a rule?
options: Something we all agree to do
questions.correctAnswer: Something we all agree to do

questions.question: Holding the rail on the stairs is mostly a rule about what?
Taking turns on the swing is mostly a rule about what?
What is the big question to ask about any rule?

options: No, a rule always stays the same
Yes, and people can ask for a change
Only if nobody notices the change
Only on the last day of school
questions.correctAnswer: Yes, and people can ask for a change

questions.question: Tell about one rule at your school and say what job it does.
questions.expectedAnswer: Any real school rule works. A strong answer names the rule and then says whether it keeps people safe or keeps things fair, and why the student thinks so.

questions.question: A friend says the biggest kid should always go first. Is that rule fair? Tell why.
questions.expectedAnswer: It is not fair, because it does not give everyone the same chance. It only helps one person, the biggest kid. A fair rule would give every person a turn.

reflections.text: Which rule at school makes the most sense to you?
Is there a rule you would like to ask about? Say it out loud.

history.title: Rule Questions Kids Ask

data.question: Why do grown-ups get to make the rules? 🤔
data.answer: Often it is their job to keep kids safe. But not always. A class can make rules together. A team can too. And kids can ask for a rule to change.

data.question: What if a rule feels unfair?
data.answer: Say so. Then say why. A reason helps a lot. Follow the rule while you ask. That way people hear the reason and not the fuss.

data.question: Are there rules everywhere? 🌍
data.answer: Yes, in every place we share. Homes and buses have them. So do parks, pools and libraries. Even a game you make up has rules.

data.question: What if someone breaks a rule?
data.answer: Then something happens next. Maybe a reminder. Maybe a turn missed. The point is not to be mean. It is to keep the rule working for all of us.

data.question: Can a rule be fair to one person and not to another? ⚖️
data.answer: Yes. That is the tricky part. It is why we ask who a rule helps. If it helps just one kid, we should talk about it.

data.question: Do rules ever go away?
data.answer: They do. A rule can end when the reason for it ends. We do not need a rule about a broken door once the door is fixed.

history.title: Investigation: One Better Rule
history.meta: 1st Grade • Investigation brief • find a rule, test it, ask for one change

data.title: One Better Rule
data.instructions: Find one rule in your classroom. Ask who it helps. Then say one way to make it better, and tell the class.
data.fitReason: A first grader learns what a rule is by testing a real one they live under, not by hearing a definition. Asking who a rule helps, out loud, in their own room, is the whole civic move in miniature.

brief.context: Your classroom already has rules. Some are on a chart. Some are just things everybody does. You may walk around and look, and you may ask your teacher what a rule is for.
brief.audience: The class, who will vote on which better rule to try for a week
brief.drivingQuestion: Does this rule help everyone, or does it help just some people?
brief.seedDirection: Pick a rule you actually follow every day, not a made-up one. Real rules are easier to test.
lockedLessonFacts: A rule is something we all agree to do.
Some rules keep us safe. Some rules keep things fair.
Asking about a rule is not the same as breaking it.
Rules can change, and people can ask for a change.
openQuestions: Who does this rule help the most?
Is anybody left out by it?
What is one small change that would help more people?
stakeholders: Everyone in your class who follows the rule
Your teacher, who has to make the rule work
A new student who does not know the rule yet
criteria: You name one real rule from your room
You say whether it keeps people safe or keeps things fair
You say one change and one reason for it
constraints: The rule has to be a real one from your room
Your change has to still be safe
brief.deliverable: A short talk to the class, with a drawing of the rule, that names the rule, says who it helps, and asks for one change.

parallelExample.context: A class had a rule that the first person to the door held it for everyone.
parallelExample.move: One student noticed the same fast kid always got there first and never got to walk through with a friend. She asked for a change: the door holder switches every day, by the class list.
parallelExample.whyItHelps: She did not say the rule was bad. She found who it left out, and changed one small part so it helped more people.
